entries.answer: A startup crash can come from signing, missing game data, incompatible settings, or an early runtime failure. Do not change several things at once. Record the build, device, OS version, signing method, and the first fatal lines in the log.

A loading crash often needs the log to distinguish memory pressure from missing or damaged data. If the crash happens after changing graphics or mods, revert that last change before doing a full reinstall.

If the launcher opens but Story Mode crashes, the failure is later in the runtime than an installation launch failure. Keep the exact point where it exits, then attach run.log and any crash report so the project can separate content, renderer, and memory causes.

A repeatable mission crash is more useful than a random crash because the trigger is consistent. Note the mission name, exact objective, character, mods enabled, and whether the same save crashes every time.
For a cutscene crash, record whether it happens before playback, during playback, or when returning to gameplay. Test the same point with mods disabled and keep the log from that attempt.
If the crash began immediately after a mod import, restore the files changed by that mod first. A clean test without the mod is more informative than changing graphics settings at the same time.
If one setting change caused the crash, return only that option to its previous value. If you changed many options together, reset the graphics profile and re-enable settings one by one.

MetalFX changes the rendering path and also adds memory cost. If enabling it causes a new crash, disable it, confirm the game is stable without it, then test a lower render resolution before enabling it again.
MSAA is expensive on mobile GPUs and memory. If a crash or severe slowdown appears only with MSAA enabled, keep it off while testing the rest of the graphics stack.

A memory-pressure termination can look like a normal force close. On 4 GB devices especially, use the low-memory path, Normal textures, conservative resolution, and the supported Increased Memory Limit route when eligible. Logs are still needed to confirm the cause.

If the app stays on the same startup screen, distinguish a true freeze from slow first-time work. Note whether audio continues, whether the UI still responds, and how long the state persists, then capture the log before force-closing.

Endless loading can be caused by missing data, a blocked file read, a mod conflict, or a runtime loop. Check whether the log continues to grow. If it stops at the same line every attempt, share the surrounding lines.

A black screen with audio is different from a full freeze. It suggests the game loop may still be alive while rendering failed. Record whether menus respond, whether the screen becomes visible after switching apps, and include the log.
A persistent white or blank frame should be treated as a rendering or surface problem until logs say otherwise. Test default graphics, disable mods, and record whether UI or audio still works.
Pink or purple surfaces usually mean a texture resource did not load correctly. Check the affected archive or mod first, especially if the issue started after changing RPF content.

Missing textures can come from damaged game data, modded archives, or streaming pressure. If they appear only after long play, note memory and heat; if they appear immediately in the same place, verify the relevant files.
Black materials can point to a shader, resource, or rendering-path issue. Test default graphics and a clean archive before changing many unrelated settings.
For flickering, identify whether the whole frame flickers or only specific objects or shadows. A full-frame issue and an object-level shader issue need different debugging evidence.

If only shadows are broken, return shadow quality and related effects to default first. If the problem remains in the same area with default settings, capture a screenshot and log with the exact location.
Reflection problems can depend on the graphics path and MSAA combination. Test the safe default reflection settings before treating it as damaged game data.
If the HUD disappears, check whether a HUD or control layout setting disabled it. If menus still work, restore the default HUD profile before reinstalling the app.
For UI clipped by the notch or screen edge, record the exact device model and orientation. A safe-area bug is device-layout specific, so screenshots are more useful than generic performance logs.
If touch targets are offset, note the device, orientation, display zoom or scaling, and whether the problem starts after rotating the phone. Reset the HUD layout before testing again.

If all game audio is missing, first check iOS output routing and volume, then restart the app without Bluetooth accessories. If only one sound category is missing, mention which category because that points to a different problem.
Audio crackle can appear when the runtime is overloaded or when the audio path itself fails. Note whether it starts together with FPS drops or happens even in light scenes.
For audio desync, note whether it only affects cutscenes and whether FPS is unstable at the same time. Reproduce it with default graphics before assuming the media files are damaged.
If a controller disconnects repeatedly, verify the Bluetooth connection outside the game first. If iOS keeps the controller connected but GTA stops reading input, capture the exact moment and build.
A crash during save can risk progress. Stop overwriting the same slot, verify free storage, back up the save container, and capture logs from the next controlled test.
If opening the pause map triggers the crash, test with pinch gestures and custom HUD settings removed. Record whether the crash happens immediately on opening the map or only after zooming.
A clothing crash can be tied to installed DLC or modded clothing data. Test with custom clothing packs disabled and record the exact item or menu category that triggers it.

If one specific vehicle triggers the crash, test another vehicle and remove vehicle mods before reinstalling the whole game. A model-specific crash often points to changed assets rather than global graphics settings.

A crash in the same map area every time can indicate an asset or streaming problem for that region. Record the location, direction of travel, vehicle speed, and whether a clean game archive reproduces it.
Random crashes need more context than repeatable ones. Track play time, heat, current mission or area, memory-heavy settings, and whether crashes become more common after the device warms up.
